prompt.context: Bob is a master brewer and has been brewing beer for the past decade. Upon graduating from Stern, he opened a brewery on the Upper West Side called Something Witty that features Belgian Witbier styled brews. While he found early success, he has noticed an increase in customers asking for gluten-free alternatives, such as cider. Bob has hired us to help him analyze his options.
prompt.question: Bob has decided to explore expansion into cider. How would you approach analyzing his options, and what are your thoughts on the two renovation scenarios shown in Exhibit 1?

clarifying_info.a: Bob's goal is to continue to be profitable regardless of what expansion opportunity he explores.

clarifying_info.q: What does Bob currently sell and how?
clarifying_info.a: Bob currently only sells bottled beer direct to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: How many bottles are in a case?
How many days does production run?
clarifying_info.a: Production runs Monday through Friday — assume 20 days per month.

exhibits.title: Bottled Beverage Production
exhibits.shows: A table comparing beer and cider production volumes and selling prices under two scenarios: Current State and After Renovations for Cider Production.

framework: Alternatives to renovation: other beverages (wine, cocktails, cider via resale), experiences (live music, themed nights), food offerings
Costs: renovations, equipment, licensing, break-even analysis
Market: market size, competitors, customer tastes/preferences, cannibalization risk
Capabilities: organic/in-house expansion (equipment, training, ingredients, space) vs. outsourcing/purchasing from another manufacturer; current capacity utilization

questions.prompt: Question 1a: What are your thoughts on the two options shown in Exhibit 1 (Current State vs. After Renovations)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize there are other expansion paths beyond renovating the existing factory (e.g., building a new facility, buying cider from an existing company and reselling). For the two options shown: Current State pros — specialization in one product yields a consistent marketing message and specialized labor; cons — fails to meet demand for gluten-free customers, no revenue upside. After Renovations pros — new product offering, cider has a higher selling price than beer; cons — beer production drops by 6 cases/day, renovation costs must be recovered.

questions.prompt: Question 1b: What will be the change in Bob's annual revenue if he begins to produce cider?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the net annual revenue impact of the renovation scenario versus current state. A strong approach calculates the revenue lost from reduced beer production and the revenue gained from new cider production. The interviewer should wait for the candidate to ask for the clarifying information (30 bottles/case, 20 days/month).

math.setup: Compare total annual revenue: After Renovations vs. Current State. Cases/day × 30 bottles/case × 20 days/month × 12 months = annual bottles. Multiply by selling price.
steps: Current beer revenue: 30 cases/day × 30 bottles × 240 days × $5.00 = $1,080,000/year
Post-renovation beer revenue: 24 cases/day × 30 bottles × 240 days × $5.00 = $864,000/year
New cider revenue: 12 cases/day × 30 bottles × 240 days × $6.00 = $518,400/year
Alternative shortcut: focus on changes only — lost beer: 6 cases/day × 30 × 240 × $5 = −$216,000; gained cider: 12 × 30 × 240 × $6 = +$518,400; net = +$302,400

questions.prompt: Question 2: Besides potential revenue, what other factors should Bob consider before expanding into the cider market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should quickly identify cost as a key factor, then broaden to other dimensions. Strong answers cover: Costs (labor training, equipment, labeling, marketing, raw materials such as apples); Market Size/Demand (cider vs. beer market size, number of new customers, expected future demand, growth rate of both markets); Go-to-Market Strategy; Impact to Core (cannibalization of beer sales, brand equity); New Distribution Channels (grocery, liquor stores).

questions.prompt: Question 3: Bob has determined that he needs to capture at least 0.5% of the NYC take-home cider market annually in order to break even. Will he be able to produce enough cider to capture that 0.5%?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the annual cider production figure from Question 1b (86,400 bottles/year). The interviewer provides the NYC market size (15.5 million bottles) only when asked. Candidate computes 0.5% of 15.5M and compares to production capacity. An excellent candidate will also note that production capacity alone does not guarantee sales — demand for Bob's cider has not been verified.

math.setup: Compare Bob's annual cider production capacity to 0.5% of the NYC take-home cider market.
steps: Bob's annual cider production: 12 cases/day × 30 bottles/case × 240 days/year = 86,400 bottles/year
86,400 > 77,500 → Bob can produce enough to meet the break-even threshold
math.answer: Yes, Bob can produce enough cider (86,400 bottles/year) to capture the required 0.5% of the NYC market (77,500 bottles/year).

brainstorming.prompt: Besides potential revenue, what other factors should Bob consider before expanding into the cider market?

categories.name: Costs
ideas: Marketing spend to promote new product
Raw materials — apples and other cider ingredients

categories.name: Market Size & Demand
ideas: Size of cider market vs. beer market in NYC
Number of new gluten-free or cider-seeking customers
Growth rate of cider market vs. beer market

categories.name: Go-to-Market Strategy
ideas: Pricing strategy for cider relative to beer
Positioning and branding of cider under Something Witty

categories.name: Impact to Core Business
ideas: Cannibalization — will cider drinkers replace beer purchases?
Brand equity — does a cider line dilute the Belgian Witbier brand identity?

recommendation: Bob should make the investment to produce cider
He will see a net increase in revenues of $302,400 per year and his production capacity of 86,400 bottles/year exceeds the 77,500-bottle break-even threshold (0.5% of the 15.5M-bottle NYC market)
risks: Uncertainty about the cider market trajectory — can Bob actually meet or sustain demand going forward?
Competitive intensity in the cider industry
Demand risk: production capacity exceeding demand does not guarantee Bob can sell 86,400 bottles
next_steps: Conduct competitive analysis of the NYC cider market
Pressure-test Bob's assumption that 0.5% market share is sufficient for break-even
Market research to identify the optimal price point, flavor profile, and packaging for maximum sales
